prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a measurement achievement of the kind that changes what can be observed. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light shift that otherwise destroys the accuracy of a trapped-atom clock, and the experimental programmes in Tokyo and Boulder then took fractional uncertainty from the 1e-16 range to about 1e-18, with systematics (blackbody shift, lattice light shifts, collisions) understood and controlled rather than merely estimated. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in many independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE, and others) and clock-to-clock comparisons agree at the 1e-18 level. It has opened new measurements that nobody could do before: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and relativistic geodesy, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, and the pending redefinition of the second. Four of the seven members who ranked it placed it in their top three or four, and the two people credited are, in my reading of all eight ballots, the least contested attribution on the whole shortlist. Timing is good: the field is mature and the SI redefinition discussion makes the recognition current rather than premature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision frequency metrology has already been honoured twice (Hall and Haensch for the comb in 2005, Wineland and Haroche in 2012 for single-ion control, including the Al+ ion clock), so a third clock-related prize could look incremental or like a technology prize rather than a discovery. The lattice clock does not reveal a new phenomenon of nature on its own; its prize case rests on the invention (the magic-wavelength concept and its realization) and on the new physics it enables, much of which is still prospective, since the redefinition of the second has not happened and the dark-matter and constants searches have so far produced bounds, not detections. Attribution is also not airtight: Lemonde's group (SYRTE), Hollberg, Ludlow and others contributed to early demonstrations and the many-body clock, and none of them is in the credited names.

responses.point: Ranks the lattice clock first on the strength of the magic-wavelength idea and the atomic-structure physics, and sees a clean two-person credit, while noting that some members may feel the comb prize of 2005 already covers the field.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and on the two-person credit, and I would go slightly further on the overlap question: the comb prize rewarded a ruler for optical frequencies, while the lattice clock is a different object, an ensemble of neutral atoms in which the dominant systematic is cancelled by design. That distinction must be written into the citation, which is why my wording stresses the lattice clock and not frequency metrology in general. Where I would press you is on the share between Katori and Ye: Katori has the concept and the first demonstration, but the 1e-18 and many-body results that made the instrument a tool for other physics come mostly from the JILA programme, so I would not accept a citation that reads as if the idea alone was the discovery.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube first as a detector-driven discovery of a new observational window, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering, while admitting that AMANDA and Baikal precursors and the size of the collaboration complicate credit.
responses.response: I respect the instrument argument; it is the one I use for the clock. I ranked IceCube last on my list for two reasons that I think remain valid after reading your ballot. First, the diffuse flux is secure but the identification of sources, which is what makes it astronomy, still rests on two or three objects at moderate significance, so the physics is still being established. Second, as you say yourself, credit within a collaboration of hundreds, with predecessor efforts, is unresolved, and my experience with large collaborations is that the three names then end up reflecting leadership roles more than an individual discovery. I would not oppose IceCube later, but I see the clock as the more finished case with a cleaner attribution.

responses.point: Places the lattice clock fourth, finds the idea original and quantitatively rigorous, but worries that overlap with the frequency-metrology prizes could make some members see it as incremental, and prefers topological insulators first.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously and have listed it as my own main reservation. My answer is that the earlier prizes did not cover this achievement: neither Hall and Haensch nor Wineland solved the problem of trapping many neutral atoms without perturbing the clock transition, and that is what allowed the stability to improve by orders of magnitude. On topological insulators, I do not doubt the originality, but the credit problem looks heavier to me than for the clock. The supplied names leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp actually tested, and in the opening ballots the 3D materials work and Mele's role keep appearing as unresolved points. I would like to hear how you propose to settle that within three names.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first and Cirac-Zoller second, arguing that the 2004 strong-coupling work is a clear new regime of light-matter physics, and openly flags her proximity to the field and that the 2025 prize may weigh against returning to superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour on proximity, and I think the 2025 point is a real constraint: the committee has just recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and circuit QED is the natural continuation, so the distinct contribution will have to be argued very carefully. B029 is also a case where, by your own account, Wallraff, who performed the strong-coupling experiment, is not among the credited names, so the experimental credit is incomplete. For Cirac and Zoller I am more sympathetic: it is a clean two-person theory prize that I list as an alternative. My doubt is that the experimental realization is a decade of work by others, so the citation would honour proposals more than demonstrated measurements, whereas the clock is both.

responses.point: Ranks the Higgs experimental discovery first as the decisive experimental verification of mass generation, with Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, but acknowledges that allocation among ATLAS, CMS and LHC leadership is contestable.
responses.response: The scientific importance of the Higgs observation is beyond dispute and I ranked it myself, but only seventh. My difficulty is the one you name: the supplied names are a choice of leaders, not of the people who made the discovery measurement, and with two experiments of thousands of members the committee would be forced to pick spokespersons. I also notice that the four of us who proposed names for it did not agree on them (Jenni and Della Negra each appear on some ballots and not on others, and only Gianotti and Virdee are common to all four), which tells me the attribution is not mature even if the science is.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the 2005 and 2012 prizes in precision spectroscopy and ion control, and whether a citation can separate the lattice clock from them convincingly.

Whether to divide the credit between Katori (concept and first demonstration) and Ye (accuracy, stability and many-body clocks) with a two-name citation, or whether early contributors such as Lemonde's group need to be mentioned in the discussion even though they cannot be named.
Whether the 2026 committee wants a measurement-instrument prize in a year when other candidates (topological insulators, moire graphene, IceCube) are discovery-driven and recent.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is at JILA and worked in Hall's group; this is a distant mentor-lineage connection and no collaboration or joint work with Ye or Katori is apparent from my profile, so I do not see a recusal issue, but I flag it for the committee. I am also a WACQT leader, which overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers, and I hold a stake in the spin-off Deep Light Vision, which is irrelevant to every shortlisted candidate. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
